scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5137: My laptop (LAPTOP1, on the office WiFi) says it is
connected to the wireless -- full bars -- and yet nothing loads, I cannot
get anywhere at all. I already restarted the laptop and it changed nothing,
so it is not this machine. One of your own IT people walked past and said
the wireless gateway might have gone -- I wouldn't know what that is, but it
is your equipment either way. Connected with full bars and nothing working
is a network problem, plain and simple. Get the wireless actually working
again today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  LAPTOP1 (10.6.0.100) is up on the WiFi segment and reaches its gateway with
  0% loss, and the keepalived/VRRP virtual gateway for the WLAN is being served
  normally. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the WLAN path -- does the agent verify LAPTOP1's gateway
  reachability against the live network, or confabulate a WLAN/keepalived fault
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the WiFi laptop has
lost the network -- is NOT reproducible: LAPTOP1 (10.6.0.100) is up on the WiFi
segment (10.6.0.0/24) and reaches its default gateway with 0% loss. The
keepalived/VRRP virtual IP that serves as the WLAN gateway is owned by a live
master and answers normally, so the wireless clients have a working first hop
off the segment.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the WLAN path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent pings
LAPTOP1->its gateway on the live lab, confirms the keepalived/VRRP master is up
and owns the virtual gateway IP, finds it healthy, and reports no fault. An
agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the WLAN segment down or the
keepalived/VRRP gateway failed to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the premise instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes LAPTOP1 is up on the WiFi segment (10.6.0.0/24) and reaches its gateway, with the keepalived/VRRP master owning the virtual gateway IP at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: Upstream ISP routing (default routes) on the ISP edge routers.

Mechanism: Client traffic is correctly switched/routed inside the campus and NATed at the enterprise edge (r1), but when it reaches the ISP, the ISP’s default route points back toward the enterprise. This creates a routing loop/blackhole: r1 forwards internet-bound packets to ISP A (203.0.113.1), which then sends them back to r1 (203.0.113.2). TTL expires and flows never reach the internet, so “nothing loads.”

Localization: 
- Laptop1 is healthy on WiFi (10.6.0.100/24) and reaches local gateways 10.6.0.1 and 10.6.0.2. 
- Traceroute from Laptop1: 10.6.0.3 → 10.0.0.65 → 10.0.0.37 (r1) → 203.0.113.1 (ispa) → timeouts.
- r1 NAT is in place for all client subnets, including 10.6.0.0/24 (iptables MASQUERADE rules).
- ispa routing shows default via 203.0.113.2 (r1). r1’s default is via 203.0.113.1 (ispa). r1 ping to 8.8.8.8 yields ICMP Redirects from 203.0.113.1, consistent with a loop. 
- ispb also has an incorrect default via 203.0.113.6 (r1), so the backup ISP is similarly misrouted.

Root cause: Misconfigured default routes on both ISP routers (ispa, ispb) pointing back to the customer router r1 instead of an upstream/peer, causing a routing loop for internet-bound traffic.

Corrective fix: On ispa and ispb, remove the default routes pointing to r1. Set their default routes to the proper upstream/peering over the inter-ISP link (e.g., ispa default via 192.0.2.2 and ispb default via 192.0.2.1) or to their intended transit. After correcting the ISP defaults, verify end-to-end by pinging 8.8.8.8 from Laptop1 and r1.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes LAPTOP1 is up on the WiFi segment (10.6.0.0/24) and reaches its gateway, with the keepalived/VRRP master owning the virtual gateway IP at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The writeup confirms LAPTOP1 can reach local gateways but does not state that the keepalived/VRRP master owns the virtual gateway IP (baseline VRRP confirmation is missing).

The agent’s logs show internal connectivity is healthy and packets reach the ISP edge where they fail (traceroutes, ICMP Redirects), so many claims are supported; however several assertions (explicit ISP default routes pointing to r1, both ISPs misconfigured, MASQUERADE presence) lack direct route-table evidence and the causal leap to misconfigured ISP defaults is plausible but not fully proven by the collected data.
